claims.claim: rotifers in Keratella and Conochilus ingest particles down to 0.5 µm (Ooms-Wilms et al. 1995; abstract only)
claims.note: full text not obtained. The abstract (not used to confirm) does not name Keratella: in eutrophic Lake Loosdrecht (April–September) the tracers were 0.51-µm microspheres and fluorescently labelled bacteria; by microspheres the highest bacterial uptake was by Filinia longiseta (May–July) and Anuraeopsis fissa (June–September), by labelled bacteria by Conochilus unicornis (June) and A. fissa (July); rotifers were much more important bacterivores than cladocerans. So this abstract supports Conochilus taking ~0.5-µm particles but says nothing of Keratella. The research note (small_zooplankton_and_microbial_loop.md, line ~547) quotes the abstract as 'K. cochlearis and Conochilus ingested only 0.5-µm particles' — not in the abstract read here (marineinfo's copy; OUP's own page could not be opened, so a human should compare). Until then the Keratella part has no source; Bogdan & Gilbert 1982, cited beside it in the code, may be the right one

claims.claim: Keratella, Kellicottia and Conochilus eat bacteria-sized food, Polyarthra and Synchaeta don't (Bogdan & Gilbert 1982; Ooms-Wilms et al. 1995)
claims.note: as above. The abstract names none of Keratella, Kellicottia, Polyarthra or Synchaeta; it adds Filinia and Anuraeopsis as the leading bacterivores in Lake Loosdrecht, which the code's list leaves out
